questions.stem: Why were surveyors' accounts of dwellings important?

answer.exemplar: They documented overcrowding and poor conditions, providing evidence that spurred public health reforms and housing regulation.

questions.explanation: Surveyors documented overcrowding and poor conditions, providing evidence for reforms. The tempting view sees only description rather than advocacy.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A public health measure and its effect
questions.stem: Why did public health measures take time to show effect?

options.text: Because measures were never implemented
Because they worked instantly in every case
Because no one ever got sick again
Because infrastructure and habits changed slowly

questions.explanation: Public health measures took time because infrastructure and habits changed slowly. Instant effect, no sickness and non-implementation are wrong.

questions.topic: A doctor's note on one street
questions.stem: What did a doctor's note on one street typically recommend?

options.text: It recommended abolishing all medicine
It recommended piped water and refuse removal
It recommended banning all children
It recommended ending all sanitation

questions.explanation: A doctor's note recommended piped water and refuse removal. Abolishing medicine, banning children and ending sanitation are wrong.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A colonial economy built on one export

stimulus.body: The colony exported cocoa almost exclusively. When blight destroyed the crop for two seasons, export revenue vanished, the government defaulted on loans and famine threatened.

questions.stem: What happened when blight destroyed the cocoa crop?

options.text: All loans were forgiven automatically
options.misconception: introduces a relief absent from the text

options.text: The colony became richer instantly
Export revenue vanished and the government defaulted
Famine was impossible

questions.explanation: Blight wiped out export revenue and caused default. Richer, forgiven loans and no famine are wrong.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a cash crop did to land use

stimulus.body: The shift to sugar cane replaced mixed farming with monoculture. Soil exhaustion followed, and the colony imported food it once grew, raising costs for labourers.

questions.stem: What followed the shift to sugar cane?

options.text: Soil fertility improved dramatically
Soil exhaustion and food imports followed
Food became free and abundant
Labourers became wealthy instantly

questions.explanation: Soil exhaustion and food imports followed. Improved fertility, free food and wealthy labourers are wrong.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What an oil concession was
questions.stem: Why were oil concessions controversial?

answer.exemplar: They gave foreign companies long-term control over a nation's key resource for limited royalties, often leaving host states with little benefit or sovereignty.

questions.explanation: Concessions gave foreign companies long-term control for limited royalties, leaving host states little benefit or sovereignty. The tempting view sees investment only.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Concession terms read closely

stimulus.body: The terms gave the company ninety-nine years of extraction rights, a low fixed royalty and freedom to export all oil. The host state could not review the terms for fifty years.

questions.stem: Which term most limited the host state?

options.text: The low royalty most limited the host state
options.misconception: partial, but the review ban is more limiting

options.text: The ninety-nine years most limited the host state
options.misconception: partial, but the review ban is more limiting

options.text: The fifty-year ban on reviewing terms most limited the host state
The export freedom most limited the host state
options.misconception: partial, but the review ban is more limiting

questions.explanation: The fifty-year ban on reviewing terms most limited the host state, though other terms also hurt. The question asks which most limited.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Coal smoke and a city's air

stimulus.body: The health report recorded soot on buildings, frequent coughs among residents and higher child mortality in smoky districts. It recommended restricting factory emissions during fog.

questions.stem: What did the report recommend?

options.text: It recommended ending all medicine
It recommended increasing factory emissions
It recommended banning all children
It recommended restricting factory emissions during fog

questions.explanation: The report recommended restricting factory emissions during fog. Increasing emissions, banning children and ending medicine are wrong.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a conservation act left out

stimulus.body: The act protected game animals but allowed farming and mining inside the reserve. Environmentalists said the omissions made protection largely symbolic.

questions.stem: Why did environmentalists criticise the act?

options.text: Because all activity was banned
Because game animals were protected
options.misconception: confuses the protected with the omitted

options.text: Because farming and mining were allowed inside the reserve
Because the reserve did not exist

questions.explanation: Environmentalists criticised allowing farming and mining inside the reserve. Protecting game, banning all activity and non-existence are wrong.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A park act read as a mechanism
questions.stem: Why did a park act need enforcement mechanisms?

answer.exemplar: Without wardens and penalties, rules against hunting and damage would be ignored, so enforcement made protection real rather than merely declared.

questions.explanation: Without wardens and penalties, rules would be ignored, so enforcement made protection real. The tempting view sees laws as self-executing.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: An agreement with no mechanism behind it
questions.stem: What makes an agreement with no mechanism weak?

options.text: The presence of binding treaties makes it weak
The presence of too many penalties makes it weak
The presence of too much enforcement makes it weak
The absence of targets, deadlines and penalties makes it weak

questions.explanation: Absence of targets, deadlines and penalties makes it weak. Too many penalties, too much enforcement and binding treaties are wrong.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A conference that produced only a declaration
questions.stem: Why might states prefer a declaration over a treaty?

answer.exemplar: A declaration lets states signal concern and build consensus without accepting binding obligations that could constrain future policy or require ratification.

questions.explanation: A declaration signals concern and builds consensus without binding obligations that could constrain policy or require ratification. The tempting view sees only failure.
